data.description:
## The defect (reproduced, not inferred)

`git grep -E` does not merely ignore `\b` — it treats it as a literal `b`, which makes the
pattern match a **different** set of lines rather than a superset. Minimal repro on
**git 2.56.0**, against a 2-line file (`alpha beta` then `alphabeta`):

| Command | Matched |
|---|---|
| `git grep --no-index -nE 'alpha\b'` | **line 2 — `alphabeta`** |
| `git grep --no-index -nP 'alpha\b'` | line 1 — `alpha beta` (correct) |
| system `grep -nE 'alpha\b'` | line 1 — `alpha beta` (correct) |

So `alpha\b` is compiled as `alphab`. The result is simultaneously a **false positive**
(it matched the one line a word-boundary search must exclude) and a **false negative**
(it missed the only line that should match). Both exits are `0`, nothing is written to
stderr, and the hit count is plausible — so the failure is completely silent.

## Why this matters more than its blast radius suggests

A tree-wide sweep found **0** occurrences in tracked files (`docs`, `scripts`, `tests`,
`src`, `.github`, `Makefile`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`), so no committed check is currently
wrong. The exposure is in **ticket acceptance criteria**, which live in the store rather
than the tree and are therefore invisible to every lint and ratchet the repo runs.

An AC of the shape "`git grep -E 'symbol\b' -- src` returns 0 hits" is the single most
common removal-verification idiom in the two complexity-reduction epics. Under this
behavior such an AC can report a clean removal while the symbol is still present, because
the pattern it actually ran was never the pattern that was written. That is a verification
gate that returns `pass` without having measured the thing it names — the same failure
class as a probe with no negative control.

## Suggested fix

Amend the author-facing AC guidance — `src/rebar/_guides/writing-a-passing-plan.md`,
surfaced as `rebar explain plan` — rather than adding a new document. The guide already
teaches how to write a verifiable AC; this is the trap that makes a verifiable-looking one
lie. Two portable replacements, either of which is correct under `-E`:

```sh
# explicit boundary classes — portable across git grep, GNU grep, and BSD grep
git grep -nE '(^|[^A-Za-z0-9_])symbol([^A-Za-z0-9_]|$)' -- src
# or switch the engine, which supports \b properly
git grep -nP 'symbol\b' -- src
```

`-F` (fixed-string) is also immune and is the better choice whenever the target is a
literal with no regex metacharacters, which covers most import-removal ACs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1 — `src/rebar/_guides/writing-a-passing-plan.md` gains guidance naming the trap, showing the observed wrong result (`alpha\b` matching `alphabeta`), and giving both portable replacements plus the `-F` note.
- [ ] AC2 — `rebar explain plan` renders that guidance (exit 0, and its output contains the replacement pattern `[^A-Za-z0-9_]`).
- [ ] AC3 — a test pins the repro so a future git version change is caught: it runs `git grep --no-index -E` and `-P` over a 2-line fixture and asserts the documented divergence, skipping cleanly if `-P` is unavailable in the host build.
- [ ] AC4 — `git grep -nF 'git grep' -- docs scripts tests src .github Makefile CONTRIBUTING.md | grep -F '\b'` still returns 0 tracked occurrences, so the fix does not itself introduce the broken idiom.
- [ ] AC5 — `make lint` and `make typecheck` exit 0.
data.title: git grep -E reads \b as a literal b, so an AC written with it silently measures the wrong thing — matching alphabeta and missing alpha beta
